q: How many interlocking rings appear on the Olympic flag?
note: The six colours, counting the white background, were chosen because every national flag of the day contained at least one of them.

q: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games, in 1896?
note: Winners there were handed a silver medal and an olive branch, as gold for first place only arrived later.

q: Which Winter Olympic sport has team-mates sweeping the ice in front of a sliding stone?
note: The granite stones weigh around 44 pounds each, and the finest have long been quarried from a single Scottish island, Ailsa Craig.

q: How many separate events make up the Olympic decathlon?
note: The name comes from the Greek for ten contests, and they are spread over two exhausting days.

q: How many years apart are the Summer Olympic Games normally held?
note: The four-year gap itself has a name, borrowed from the ancient Greeks: an Olympiad.

q: In which country were the ancient Olympic Games held?
note: They took place at Olympia in honour of Zeus, with the first recorded games traditionally dated to 776 BC.

q: The traditional Olympic motto is Faster, Higher, and which third word?
note: In the original Latin it is Citius, Altius, Fortius, and a fourth word meaning Together was added in 2021.

q: Which Spanish city hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics?
note: Its opening ceremony ended with an archer firing a flaming arrow over the cauldron to light it.

q: How many miles long is an Olympic marathon?
note: The oddly precise distance was fixed after the 1908 London Games and made the official standard in 1921.

q: Which Winter Olympic sport combines cross-country skiing with rifle shooting?
note: Competitors shoot both lying down and standing up, and every miss costs them a penalty loop or a time penalty.

q: Which Olympic sport is contested with weapons called the foil, the epee and the sabre?
note: The three weapons have different target areas, and with the epee the entire body counts.

q: Which French alpine town hosted the first Winter Olympics, in 1924?
note: It was billed at the time as an International Winter Sports Week and only later recognised as the first Winter Games.

q: The Olympic Games of 1940 and 1944 were cancelled because of what?
note: Tokyo had been due to host in 1940, and it eventually got its Games 24 years later.

q: In which Olympic sliding sport do athletes race head-first down an ice track?
note: Its close cousin the luge is raced feet-first, which competitors insist is the less frightening option.

q: Which Japanese city became the first Asian host of the Summer Olympics, in 1964?
note: The country opened its first bullet train line just nine days before the opening ceremony.

q: Which Brazilian city hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics, the first held in South America?
note: Golf returned to the programme at those Games after an absence of well over a century.

q: Which French baron founded the modern Olympic Games?
note: He also designed the five-ring flag, and his heart is buried at ancient Olympia.

q: Olympic gold medals are made mostly of which metal?
note: They are silver medals with a thin gold plating, as the last solid gold ones were handed out in 1912.

q: Which Winter Olympic event combines ski jumping with cross-country skiing?
note: It has appeared at every Winter Olympics since the very first Games in 1924.

q: The three curved shapes that form the symbol of the Paralympic Games are known by what name?
note: Agito is Latin for I move, which chimes with the Paralympic motto, Spirit in Motion.

q: How many players from each team are on the field at the kickoff of a soccer match?
note: The goalkeeper is one of the eleven, and a match cannot continue if a side is reduced to fewer than seven players.

q: In soccer, which player is allowed to handle the ball inside their own penalty area?
note: The keeper is also the only player required to wear a colour that stands out from both teams and the officials.

q: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football?
note: Despite the name, the ball never has to touch the ground, which is a leftover from the sport's rugby ancestry.

q: What is the name of the National Football League's championship game?
note: The name was coined by an owner who had watched his children bouncing a toy called a Super Ball.

q: In soccer, what colour card does a referee show to send a player off the field?
note: An English referee came up with the yellow and red system after being stuck at a traffic light.

q: Which position in American football normally throws the ball to the receivers?
note: The name simply describes where he lines up behind the front line, alongside the half-back and full-back.

q: A standard soccer match is played as two halves of how many minutes each?
note: The clock never stops, so the referee adds stoppage time at the end of each half instead.

q: In soccer, what is the term for one player scoring three goals in a single match?
note: The phrase was borrowed from cricket, where a bowler who took three wickets in three balls was rewarded with a hat.

q: Which country hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup, in 1930?
note: They built a new stadium for the tournament and beat neighbours Argentina four goals to two in the final.

q: England won the men's soccer World Cup for the first time in which year?
note: They beat West Germany four goals to two after extra time at Wembley, on home soil.

q: How many points is a successful field goal worth in American football?
note: The same kick between the posts is worth only one point when taken straight after a touchdown.

q: How many yards separate the two goal lines on an American football field?
note: Adding the two end zones of ten yards each makes the painted field 120 yards long in total.

q: In American football, a team has four downs to advance the ball how many yards?
note: Making them resets the count, which is why commentators are forever saying first and ten.

q: What is the name of the governing body of world soccer, headquartered in Zurich?
note: It was founded in Paris in 1904 by seven European associations, none of them British.

q: Which soccer rule disallows a goal because the attacker was too far forward when the ball was played to them?
note: A player can never be caught by it from a throw-in, a corner or a goal kick.

q: What is the name of the trophy handed to the winners of the Super Bowl?
note: It is made of sterling silver by the jeweller Tiffany and shaped like a football standing on a tee.

q: In soccer, how many yards from the goal line is the penalty spot?
note: The penalty kick was introduced in 1891, and the goalkeeper must keep part of one foot on the line until the ball is struck.

q: In American football, what is the name for a long, desperate pass thrown towards the end zone as time runs out?
note: The phrase caught on after a 1975 playoff game in which the winning quarterback said he threw it and said a prayer.

q: Super Bowls are traditionally identified by numbers written in which form?
note: The fiftieth game broke the habit and used the ordinary figure 50, because a lone letter L looked odd on the merchandise.

q: In American football, what is the two-point score called when a ball carrier is tackled in his own end zone?
note: It is the only score in the game worth two points on its own, and the scoring team gets the ball back afterwards.

q: How many players from one team are on the court during a basketball game?
note: The very first game, in 1891, was played nine a side because that was how many students turned up.

q: In baseball, how many strikes make a strikeout?
note: A foul ball counts as a strike, but it cannot be the third one unless the batter was bunting.

q: What is the name of Major League Baseball's championship series?
note: The first one was played in 1903 between Boston and Pittsburgh, and Boston won it.

q: In basketball, how many points is a free throw worth?
note: A basket from open play is worth two, or three from behind the arc, a line the NBA only adopted in 1979.

q: How many innings are there in a regulation Major League Baseball game?
note: Baseball has no clock at all, so a tied game simply carries on into extra innings.

q: In ice hockey, what is the name of the hard rubber disc that players shoot at the goal?
note: Pucks are frozen before a game because a warm one bounces awkwardly on the ice.

q: How many players from each team, including the goaltender, are on the ice in ice hockey?
note: Trailing teams often pull the goaltender for an extra attacker in the closing minute, leaving the net empty.

q: How high above the floor is the rim of a basketball hoop?
note: It has not moved since 1891, even though the players have grown a great deal taller since then.

q: In baseball, what is the term for a home run hit while all three bases are occupied?
note: It brings home four runs at once, the most that can be scored on a single swing.

q: In baseball, how many balls does a batter need to be awarded a walk?
note: It is officially recorded as a base on balls, and the batter simply strolls to first.

q: What is the name of the trophy awarded to the champions of the National Hockey League?
note: Every winning player's name is engraved on it, so the trophy carries thousands of names.

q: Which small New York town is home to the Baseball Hall of Fame?
note: It was chosen because of a legend that baseball was invented there, a story historians long ago debunked.

q: During the seventh-inning stretch, baseball crowds traditionally sing which song?
a: Take Me Out to the Ball Game
accept: Take Me Out to the Ballgame
note: It was written in 1908 by two men who, by their own account, had never been to a baseball game.

q: The American college basketball tournament held each spring is popularly known by what name?
note: It is knockout from the first whistle, so a single bad afternoon ends a team's season.

q: Which exhibition basketball team is famous for comic routines performed to the tune Sweet Georgia Brown?
note: Despite the name they were founded in Chicago, and only later borrowed Harlem for its showbusiness ring.

q: Which horse race is run each May at Churchill Downs in Louisville, Kentucky?
note: It is nicknamed the Run for the Roses, and the whole thing is over in about two minutes.

q: Which Canadian-American teacher invented basketball in 1891 using two peach baskets?
note: His first game used a soccer ball, and somebody had to fetch it out of the basket after every score.

q: How many feet apart are the bases on a Major League Baseball diamond?
note: That distance has barely changed since the 1850s and is often called the most perfect number in sport.

q: The winner of which American motor race traditionally drinks a bottle of milk in victory lane?
note: The custom began in 1936 when the winner asked for buttermilk, which he drank at home on hot days.

q: What is the name of the trophy presented to the champions of the National Basketball Association?
note: It is a gold-plated ball dropping into a net, named after a former commissioner of the league.

q: In tennis, what word is used for a score of zero?
note: One popular explanation traces it to the French for egg, l'oeuf, after the shape of a nought on the scoreboard.

q: How many holes make up a full round of golf?
note: St Andrews settled on eighteen in 1764 and the rest of the golfing world simply copied it.

q: What is the feathered projectile hit back and forth in badminton called?
note: A traditional shuttlecock uses sixteen goose feathers, all taken from the same wing so it spins true.

q: In motor racing, which flag is waved as the winner crosses the finish line?
note: Its origins are murky, but the black and white squares have been ending American races since the early 1900s.

q: In a relay race, what is the object handed from one runner to the next?
note: Dropping it is bad enough, but handing it over outside the marked zone disqualifies the whole team.

q: In boxing, a referee counts to what number over a floored fighter to complete a knockout?
note: A referee can also give a standing eight count, pausing the bout to check whether a dazed fighter can continue.

q: In tennis, what term describes a game score of forty all?
note: From there a player must win two points in a row, and the word is thought to come from the French for two.

q: In golf, what is a score of one stroke under par on a hole called?
note: Two under is an eagle and three under an albatross, so the birds get grander as the scores get better.

q: In cricket, how many balls are bowled in an over?
note: Australia experimented with eight-ball overs for decades before finally falling into line in the late 1970s.

q: Which cycling race dresses its overall leader in a yellow jersey?
note: The jersey is yellow because the newspaper that founded the race was printed on yellow paper.

q: In volleyball, how many times may a team touch the ball before it must go back over the net?
note: The classic sequence has a name for each touch: the dig, the set and the spike.

q: In rugby, what is the name of the score awarded for grounding the ball behind the opponents' goal line?
note: It is called a try because it originally scored nothing at all, and merely earned a try at kicking a goal.

q: Which of the four tennis Grand Slam tournaments is played on grass?
note: The French Open is played on clay, while the Australian and US Opens use hard courts.

q: In gymnastics, what is the name of the narrow raised apparatus about four inches wide?
note: It is five metres long and stands over a metre off the floor, which is quite far enough to fall.

q: Which athletics event involves pushing a heavy metal ball from the shoulder as far as possible?
note: The men's shot weighs sixteen pounds, and throwing rather than pushing it is a foul.

q: In alpine skiing, what is the name of the event in which racers weave between closely set poles?
note: The word was borrowed from Norwegian, where it roughly means sloping track.

q: Which stroke is swum first in an individual medley race?
note: The order then runs backstroke, breaststroke and freestyle, so swimmers begin with the most punishing stroke.

q: In cricket, what is the term for a batter being dismissed without scoring a single run?
note: Going out to the very first ball you face is a golden duck, and failing to score in both innings is a pair.

q: In rowing, what is the title of the crew member who steers the boat and calls the rhythm?
note: The cox is the only one facing forwards, since the rowers travel backwards the entire way.

q: In modern competitive table tennis, a game is won by the first player to reach how many points?
note: Games ran to twenty-one until 2001, when the shorter format was brought in to make matches better television.

q: Which boxer, born Cassius Clay, lit the Olympic cauldron at the 1996 Atlanta Games?
note: His hands shook badly from Parkinson's disease as he held the torch, and the stadium fell silent.

q: Which basketball star played alongside Bugs Bunny in the 1996 film Space Jam?
note: He had briefly quit basketball to play minor league baseball two years before making the film.

q: Which Brazilian soccer legend was born Edson Arantes do Nascimento?
note: He never much liked the nickname, which a schoolfriend seems to have coined as a joke.

q: Which Jamaican sprinter won the Olympic 100 metres title in 2008, 2012 and 2016?
note: At six foot five he was considered far too tall to be a great sprinter, right up until he was one.

q: Which heavyweight boxer was nicknamed Iron Mike?
note: He kept racing pigeons as a boy in Brooklyn and still kept them at the height of his fame.

q: Which American swimmer won eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics?
note: One of the eight was won by a hundredth of a second, on a final lunge for the wall.

q: Which American sprinter won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics?
note: His victories embarrassed a Games staged as a showcase for Nazi racial theories.

q: Which Argentine footballer scored the Hand of God goal against England in 1986?
note: Four minutes after punching that one in, he ran half the length of the field to score a goal often called the greatest ever.

q: Which player broke Major League Baseball's colour barrier when he joined the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947?
note: His number 42 is retired across every team in the sport, the only number to be so honoured.

q: Which baseball slugger was nicknamed the Bambino and the Sultan of Swat?
note: He began his career as a star pitcher for Boston before being sold to the Yankees and remade as a hitter.

q: Which Englishman ran the first mile in under four minutes, in 1954?
note: He was a medical student who trained in his lunch hours, and his record was beaten just 46 days later.

q: In the 1980 Miracle on Ice, the American ice hockey team beat which country?
note: It was not the final, and the young Americans still had to beat Finland two days later to take the gold.

q: Which Canadian ice hockey player was known as The Great One?
note: His father built him a backyard rink in Ontario so he could skate every evening through the winter.

q: Which American tennis player is remembered for yelling You cannot be serious at umpires?
note: The outburst came at Wimbledon in 1981, and he later used the line as the title of his autobiography.

q: Which golfer won the 1997 Masters by twelve strokes at the age of twenty-one?
note: He became the youngest man to win the tournament, and courses around the world were lengthened in response to him.

q: Which Romanian gymnast scored the first perfect ten in Olympic history, at Montreal in 1976?
note: The scoreboard could not display a ten, so her mark flashed up as 1.00 and the crowd had to be told what it meant.

q: Which tennis player beat Bobby Riggs in the 1973 Battle of the Sexes match?
note: She won in straight sets in front of a Houston crowd of over thirty thousand, and millions more on television.

q: Which president handed over the trophy at the 1995 Rugby World Cup final wearing a Springbok jersey?
note: The green jersey had been a symbol of apartheid, and his wearing it was the point of the gesture.

q: Which horse won the American Triple Crown in 1973, taking the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths?
note: A post-mortem found his heart was more than twice the size of an average thoroughbred's.

q: Which British ski jumper became a crowd favourite at the 1988 Calgary Olympics despite finishing last?
note: He was a plasterer who funded himself, wore borrowed kit, and was so short-sighted his goggles fogged over on the way down.

q: In chess, which piece moves in an L-shape and can jump over other pieces?
note: It is the only piece that can leap, and it always lands on a square of the opposite colour to the one it left.

q: How many cards are in a standard deck, not counting the jokers?
note: Four suits of thirteen, which people have long enjoyed matching to the four seasons and the weeks of the year.

q: How many pins are set up at the start of a frame in ten-pin bowling?
note: The game is said to have grown out of nine-pin bowling after several American states banned that version in the 1800s.

q: How many squares are there on a chessboard?
note: The old legend of doubling a grain of wheat on each square ends with more wheat than the world has ever grown.

q: In the game of eight-ball pool, which ball must be potted last?
note: Potting it too early loses the game on the spot, no matter how far ahead you were.

q: How many coloured faces does a standard Rubik's Cube have?
note: Its Hungarian inventor built it as an architecture teaching aid and then took about a month to solve it himself.

q: In bowling, what is the term for three consecutive strikes?
note: Nineteenth-century tournaments handed out a live turkey to any bowler who managed it.

q: In darts, what is the highest score possible with three darts?
note: It takes three darts into the treble twenty, a target bed barely wider than a pencil.

q: In Monopoly, how much money do you collect for passing Go?
note: The board's properties are named after real streets in Atlantic City, New Jersey.

q: In chess, what is the term for a position where a player has no legal move but is not in check?
note: It counts as a draw, so a hopelessly losing player can sometimes escape with half a point.

q: How many letter tiles does each player keep on their rack in Scrabble?
note: Using all seven in a single turn earns a fifty-point bonus, known to players as a bingo.

q: In poker, what is the name of a hand containing three of a kind plus a pair?
note: It beats a flush and a straight, but loses to four of a kind.

q: In checkers, also called draughts, how many pieces does each player start with?
note: A piece that reaches the far side is crowned a king and may then move backwards as well as forwards.

q: What is the score for a perfect game in ten-pin bowling?
note: It takes twelve strikes in a row, because the tenth frame awards two bonus balls.

q: In Trivial Pursuit, what are the coloured pieces you collect for correct answers called?
note: The game was invented in 1979 by two Canadian journalists, and the orange wedge is Sports and Leisure.

q: In Britain, the card game Americans call solitaire is usually known by what name?
note: In Britain, solitaire more often means the puzzle played with pegs on a board.

q: How many red balls are on the table at the start of a frame of snooker?
note: With the six colours, that makes a maximum possible break of 147 points.

q: How many triangular points are there on a backgammon board?
note: Six to a quadrant, on a game whose ancestors were being played in the ancient Middle East thousands of years ago.

q: Which American beat Boris Spassky to take the 1972 World Chess Championship in Reykjavik?
note: Billed as the Match of the Century, it turned a Cold War chess final into front-page news worldwide.

q: How many tiles are in a standard double-six set of dominoes?
note: That is every possible pairing of the numbers from blank to six, with no combination repeated.
